{{short description|Divergent series}}

[[File:Sum1234Summary.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|The first four partial sums of the series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}. The [[parabola]] is their smoothed [[asymptote]]; its [[y-intercept|''y''-intercept]] is −1/12.<ref name="Tao" /> |alt=A graph depicting the series with layered boxes and a parabola that dips just below the ''y''-axis]]

The infinite series whose terms are the [[positive integer]]s '''{{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}''' is a [[divergent series]]. The ''n''th partial sum of the series is the [[triangular number]]

<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2},</math>

which increases without bound as ''n'' goes to [[infinity]]. Because the [[sequence]] of partial sums fails to [[Limit of a sequence|converge to a finite limit]], the [[series (mathematics)|series]] does not have a sum.

While the series itself diverges to infinity, in certain mathematical contexts it can be assigned a finite value. In particular, the methods of [[zeta function regularization]] and [[Ramanujan summation]] assign the series a value of {{sfrac|−|1|12}}, which is expressed by the famous formula<ref>{{cite book|last=Lepowsky |first=J. |year=1999 |editor=Naihuan Jing and Kailash C. Misra |chapter=Vertex operator algebras and the zeta function |title=Recent Developments in Quantum Affine Algebras and Related Topics |series=Contemporary Mathematics |volume=248 |pages=327–340 |arxiv=math/9909178 |bibcode=1999math......9178L }}.</ref>

<math display="block">1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + \cdots = -\frac{1}{12},</math>

where the left-hand side has to be interpreted as being the value obtained by using one of the aforementioned methods and not as the sum of an [[infinite series]] in its usual meaning. These methods have applications in other fields such as [[complex analysis]], [[quantum field theory]], and [[string theory]].<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Tong |first=David |date=February 23, 2012 |title=String Theory |eprint=0908.0333 | pages=28–48 |class=hep-th }}</ref>

In a monograph on [[moonshine theory]], [[University of Alberta]] mathematician Terry Gannon calls this equation "one of the most remarkable formulae in science".<ref>{{Citation |last=Gannon |first=Terry |date=April 2010 |title=Moonshine Beyond the Monster: The Bridge Connecting Algebra, Modular Forms and Physics |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0521141888 |page=140}}.</ref>

== Partial sums ==
{{Main|Triangular number}}

[[File:First six triangular numbers.svg|thumb|The first six triangular numbers]]

The partial sums of the series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + ⋯}} are {{nowrap|1, 3, 6, 10, 15}}, etc. The ''n''th partial sum is given by a simple formula:

<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n + 1)}{2}.</math>

This equation was known to the [[Pythagoreans]] as early as the sixth century BCE.<ref>{{cite book |last=Pengelley |first=David J. |year=2002 |chapter=The bridge between the continuous and the discrete via original sources |editor=Otto Bekken |title=Study the Masters: The Abel-Fauvel Conference |publisher=National Center for Mathematics Education, University of Gothenburg, Sweden |isbn=978-9185143009 |page=3 |display-editors=etal}}</ref> Numbers of this form are called [[triangular number]]s, because they can be arranged as an equilateral triangle.

The infinite sequence of triangular numbers diverges to +∞, so by definition, the infinite series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} also diverges to +∞. The divergence is a simple consequence of the form of the series: the terms do not approach zero, so the series diverges by the [[term test]].

== Summability ==
Among the classical divergent series, {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} is relatively difficult to manipulate into a finite value. Many [[summation method]]s are used to assign numerical values to divergent series, some more powerful than others. For example, [[Cesàro summation]] is a well-known method that sums [[Grandi's series]], the mildly divergent series {{nowrap|1 − 1 + 1 − 1 + ⋯}}, to {{sfrac|2}}. [[Abel summation]] is a more powerful method that not only sums Grandi's series to {{sfrac|1|2}}, but also sums the trickier series {{nowrap|[[1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯]]}} to {{sfrac|1|4}}.

Unlike the above series, {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} is not Cesàro summable nor Abel summable. Those methods work on oscillating divergent series, but they cannot produce a finite answer for a series that diverges to +∞.{{sfn|Hardy|1949|p=10}} Most of the more elementary definitions of the sum of a divergent series are stable and linear, and any method that is both stable and linear cannot sum {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯}} to a finite value {{crossreference|(see {{section link||Heuristics}} below)}}. More advanced methods are required, such as [[zeta function regularization]] or [[Ramanujan summation]]. It is also possible to argue for the value of {{sfrac|−|1|12}} using some rough heuristics related to these methods.

=== Heuristics ===
[[File:Ramanujan Notebook 1 Chapter 8 on 1234 series.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|Passage from [[Srinivasa Ramanujan|Ramanujan]]'s first notebook describing the "constant" of the series]]

[[Srinivasa Ramanujan]] presented two derivations of "{{nowrap|1=1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯ = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}" in chapter 8 of his first notebook.<ref>{{cite book |title=Ramanujan's Notebooks |url=http://www.imsc.res.in/~rao/ramanujan/NoteBooks/NoteBook1/chapterVIII/page3.htm |access-date=January 26, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=Wazir Hasan |last=Abdi |year=1992 |title=Toils and triumphs of Srinivasa Ramanujan, the man and the mathematician |publisher=National |page=41}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first=Bruce C. |last=Berndt |year=1985 |title=Ramanujan's Notebooks: Part 1 |publisher=Springer |pages=135–136}}</ref> The simpler argument proceeds in two steps, as follows.

The first key insight is that the series of positive numbers {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} closely resembles the [[alternating series]] {{nowrap|[[1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯]].}} The latter series is also divergent, but it is much easier to work with; there are several classical methods that assign it a value, which have been explored since the 18th century.<ref>{{cite web |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |translator1-first=Lucas |translator1-last=Willis |translator2-first=Thomas J. |translator2-last=Osler |title=Translation with notes of Euler's paper: Remarks on a beautiful relation between direct as well as reciprocal power series |year=2006 |publisher=The Euler Archive |url=http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~euler/pages/E352.html |access-date=2007-03-22}} Originally published as {{cite journal |last=Euler |first=Leonhard |title=Remarques sur un beau rapport entre les séries des puissances tant directes que réciproques |language=fr |journal=Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences de Berlin |year=1768 |volume=17 |pages=83–106}}</ref>

In order to transform the series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} into {{nowrap|1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯}}, one can subtract 4 from the second term, 8 from the fourth term, 12 from the sixth term, and so on. The total amount to be subtracted is {{nowrap|4 + 8 + 12 + 16 + ⋯}}, which is 4 times the original series. These relationships can be expressed using algebra. Whatever the "sum" of the series might be, call it {{nowrap|1=''c'' = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯.}} Then multiply this equation by 4 and subtract the second equation from the first:
<math display="block">
\begin{alignat}{7}
 c      = {}&& 1 + 2 &&{} + 3 + 4 &&{} + 5 + 6 + \cdots \\
 4c     = {}&&     4 &&{}     + 8 &&{}    + 12 + \cdots \\
 c - 4c = {}&& 1 - 2 &&{} + 3 - 4 &&{} + 5 - 6 + \cdots
\end{alignat}
</math>

The second key insight is that the alternating series {{nowrap|1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯}} is the formal [[power series]] expansion (for ''x'' at point 0) of the function {{sfrac|1|(1 + ''x'')<sup>2</sup>}} which is {{nowrap|1 − 2''x'' + 3''x''<sup>2</sup> − 4''x''<sup>3</sup> + ⋯}} evaluated with ''x'' defined as 1. Accordingly, Ramanujan writes
<math display="block">
 -3c = 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 + \cdots = \frac{1}{(1 + 1)^2} = \frac14.
</math>

Dividing both sides by −3, one gets ''c''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{sfrac|−|1|12}}.

Generally speaking, it is incorrect to manipulate infinite series as if they were finite sums. For example, if zeroes are inserted into arbitrary positions of a divergent series, it is possible to arrive at results that are not self-consistent, let alone consistent with other methods. In particular, the step {{nowrap|1=4''c'' = 0 + 4 + 0 + 8 + ⋯}} is not justified by the [[additive identity]] law alone. For an extreme example, prepending a single zero to the front of the series can lead to a different result.<ref name="Tao" />

One way to remedy this situation, and to constrain the places where zeroes may be inserted, is to keep track of each term in the series by attaching a dependence on some function.<ref>Promoting numbers to functions is identified as one of two broad classes of summation methods, including Abel and Borel summation, by {{cite book |last=Knopp |first=Konrad |author-link=Konrad Knopp |title=Theory and Application of Infinite Series |url=https://archive.org/details/theoryapplicatio00knop_448 |url-access=limited |year=1990 |orig-year=1922 |publisher=Dover |isbn=0-486-66165-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/theoryapplicatio00knop_448/page/n487 475]–476}}</ref> In the series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}, each term ''n'' is just a number. If the term ''n'' is promoted to a function ''n''<sup>''−s''</sup>, where ''s'' is a complex variable, then one can ensure that only like terms are added. The resulting series may be manipulated in a more rigorous fashion, and the variable ''s'' can be set to −1 later. The implementation of this strategy is called [[zeta function regularization]].

=== Zeta function regularization ===
[[File:Zeta plot.gif|thumb|upright=1.4|Plot of {{math|''ζ''(''s'')}}. For {{math|''s'' > 1}}, the series converges and {{math|''ζ''(''s'') > 1}}. Analytic continuation around the pole at {{math|1=''s'' = 1}} leads to a region of negative values, including {{math|1=''ζ''(−1) = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}.]]

In [[zeta function regularization]], the series <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty n</math> is replaced by the series <math display="inline">\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}.</math> The latter series is an example of a [[Dirichlet series]]. When the real part of {{mvar|s}} is greater than 1, the Dirichlet series converges, and its sum is the [[Riemann zeta function]] {{math|''ζ''(''s'')}}. On the other hand, the Dirichlet series diverges when the real part of {{mvar|s}} is less than or equal to 1, so, in particular, the series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} that results from setting {{math|1=''s'' = −1}} does not converge. The benefit of introducing the Riemann zeta function is that it can be defined for other values of {{mvar|s}} by [[analytic continuation]]. One can then define the zeta-regularized sum of {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} to be {{math|''ζ''(−1)}}.

From this point, there are a few ways to prove that {{math|1=''ζ''(−1) = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}. One method, along the lines of Euler's reasoning,<ref>{{cite book |first=Jeffrey |last=Stopple |year=2003 |title=A Primer of Analytic Number Theory: From Pythagoras to Riemann |isbn=0-521-81309-3 |page=202 |publisher=Cambridge University Press }}.</ref> uses the relationship between the Riemann zeta function and the [[Dirichlet eta function]] {{math|''η''(''s'')}}. The eta function is defined by an alternating Dirichlet series, so this method parallels the earlier heuristics. Where both Dirichlet series converge, one has the identities:

<math display="block">
\begin{alignat}{7}
\zeta(s)&{}={}&1^{-s}+2^{-s}&&{}+3^{-s}+4^{-s}&&{}+5^{-s}+6^{-s}+\cdots& \\
2\times2^{-s}\zeta(s)&{}={}&  2\times2^{-s}&&  {}+2\times4^{-s}&&{} +2\times6^{-s}+\cdots& \\
\left(1-2^{1-s}\right)\zeta(s)&{}={}&1^{-s}-2^{-s}&&{}+3^{-s}-4^{-s}&&{}+5^{-s}-6^{-s}+\cdots&=\eta(s).
\end{alignat}
</math>

The identity <math>(1 - 2^{1-s}) \zeta(s) = \eta(s)</math> continues to hold when both functions are extended by analytic continuation to include values of {{mvar|s}} for which the above series diverge. Substituting {{math|''s'' {{=}} −1}}, one gets {{math|1=−3''ζ''(−1) = ''η''(−1)}}. Now, computing {{math|''η''(−1)}} is an easier task, as the eta function is equal to the Abel sum of its defining series,<ref>{{cite book |last=Knopp |first=Konrad |author-link=Konrad Knopp |title=Theory and Application of Infinite Series |url=https://archive.org/details/theoryapplicatio00knop_448 |url-access=limited |year=1990 |orig-year=1922 |publisher=Dover |isbn=0-486-66165-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/theoryapplicatio00knop_448/page/n502 490]–492}}
</ref> which is a [[one-sided limit]]:

<math display="block">
 -3\zeta(-1) =
 \eta(-1) = \lim_{x\to 1^-} \left(1 - 2x + 3x^2 - 4x^3 + \cdots\right) =
 \lim_{x\to 1^-}\frac{1}{(1 + x)^2} =
 \frac14.
</math>

Dividing both sides by −3, one gets {{math|1=''ζ''(−1) = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}.

=== Cutoff regularization ===
{{Multiple image
|image1=Sum1234Plain.svg |alt1=A graph depicting the series with layered boxes |caption1=The series {{nowrap|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}
|image2=Sum1234Smoothed.svg |alt2=A graph depicting the smoothed series with layered curving stripes |caption2=After smoothing
}}
[[File:Sum1234Asymptote.svg|thumb|Asymptotic behavior of the smoothing. The ''y''-intercept of the parabola is {{sfrac|−|1|12}}.<ref name="Tao">{{Citation |first=Terence |last=Tao |author-link=Terence Tao |date=April 10, 2010 |title=The Euler–Maclaurin formula, Bernoulli numbers, the zeta function, and real-variable analytic continuation |url=http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/04/10/the-euler-maclaurin-formula-bernoulli-numbers-the-zeta-function-and-real-variable-analytic-continuation/ |access-date=January 30, 2014}}.</ref> |alt=A graph showing a parabola that dips just below the y-axis]]

The method of regularization using a [[cutoff function]] can "smooth" the series to arrive at {{sfrac|−|1|12}}. Smoothing is a conceptual bridge between zeta function regularization, with its reliance on [[complex analysis]], and Ramanujan summation, with its shortcut to the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula]]. Instead, the method operates directly on conservative transformations of the series, using methods from [[real analysis]].

The idea is to replace the ill-behaved discrete series <math>\textstyle\sum_{n=0}^N n</math> with a smoothed version

<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^\infty nf\left(\frac{n}{N}\right),</math>

where ''f'' is a cutoff function with appropriate properties. The cutoff function must be normalized to {{math|1=''f''(0) = 1}}; this is a different normalization from the one used in differential equations. The cutoff function should have enough bounded derivatives to smooth out the wrinkles in the series, and it should decay to 0 faster than the series grows. For convenience, one may require that {{mvar|f}} is [[smooth function|smooth]], [[bounded function|bounded]], and [[compactly supported]]. One can then prove that this smoothed sum is [[asymptotic]] to {{math|{{sfrac|−|1|12}} + ''CN''<sup>2</sup>}}, where {{mvar|C}} is a constant that depends on {{mvar|f}}. The constant term of the asymptotic expansion does not depend on {{mvar|f}}: it is necessarily the same value given by analytic continuation,&nbsp;{{math|{{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}.<ref name="Tao" />

=== Ramanujan summation ===
The [[Ramanujan summation|Ramanujan sum]] of {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} is also&nbsp;{{math|{{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}. Ramanujan wrote in his second letter to [[G. H. Hardy]], dated 27 February 1913:

{{blockquote|Dear Sir, I am very much gratified on perusing your letter of the 8th February 1913. I was expecting a reply from you similar to the one which a Mathematics Professor at London wrote asking me to study carefully [[Thomas John I'Anson Bromwich|Bromwich]]'s ''Infinite Series'' and not fall into the pitfalls of divergent series. ... I told him that the sum of an infinite number of terms of the series: {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯ {{=}} {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}} under my theory. If I tell you this you will at once point out to me the lunatic asylum as my goal. I dilate on this simply to convince you that you will not be able to follow my methods of proof if I indicate the lines on which I proceed in a single letter.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Of5G0r6DQiEC&pg=PA53 |page=53|title=Ramanujan: Letters and Commentary |isbn=9780821891254 |last1=Aiyangar |first1=Srinivasa Ramanujan |date=7 September 1995 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. }}</ref>}}

Ramanujan summation is a method to isolate the constant term in the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula]] for the partial sums of a series. For a function {{mvar|f}}, the classical Ramanujan sum of the series <math>\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^\infty f(k)</math> is defined as

<math display="block">c = -\frac{1}{2} f(0) - \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{B_{2k}}{(2k)!} f^{(2k-1)}(0),</math>

where {{math|''f''<sup>(2''k''−1)</sup>}} is the (2''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)th derivative of {{mvar|f}} and {{math|''B''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} is the (2''k'')th [[Bernoulli number]]: {{math|1=''B''<sub>2</sub> = {{sfrac|1|6}}}}, {{math|1=''B''<sub>4</sub> = {{sfrac|−|1|30}}}}, and so on. Setting {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = ''x''}}, the first derivative of {{mvar|f}} is 1, and every other term vanishes, so<ref name="Berndt 1985 13,134">{{Citation |first=Bruce C. |last=Berndt |year=1985 |title=Ramanujan's Notebooks: Part 1 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |pages=13, 134}}.</ref>

<math display="block">c = -\frac16 \times \frac{1}{2!} = -\frac{1}{12}.</math>

To avoid inconsistencies, the modern theory of Ramanujan summation requires that {{mvar|f}} is "regular" in the sense that the higher-order derivatives of {{mvar|f}} decay quickly enough for the remainder terms in the Euler–Maclaurin formula to tend to 0. Ramanujan tacitly assumed this property.<ref name="Berndt 1985 13,134"/> The regularity requirement prevents the use of Ramanujan summation upon spaced-out series like {{nowrap|0 + 2 + 0 + 4 + ⋯}}, because no regular function takes those values. Instead, such a series must be interpreted by zeta function regularization. For this reason, Hardy recommends "great caution" when applying the Ramanujan sums of known series to find the sums of related series.{{sfn|Hardy|1949|p=346}}

=== Failure of stable linear summation methods ===
{{See also|1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯}}
A summation method that is [[Divergent series#Properties of summation methods|linear and stable]] cannot sum the series {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯}} to any finite value. (Stable means that adding a term at the beginning of the series increases the sum by the value of the added term.) This can be seen as follows. If

<math display="block">1+2+3+\cdots=x,</math>

then adding 0 to both sides gives

<math display="block">0+1+2+3+\cdots=0+x=x</math>

by stability.  By linearity, one may subtract the second equation from the first (subtracting each component of the second line from the first line in columns) to give

<math display="block">1+1+1+\cdots=x-x=0.</math>

Adding 0 to both sides again gives

<math display="block">0+1+1+1+\cdots=0,</math>

and subtracting the last two series gives

<math display="block">1+0+0+0+\cdots=0,</math>

contradicting stability.

Therefore, every method that gives a finite value to the sum {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + ⋯}} is not stable or not linear.<ref>{{citation |last1=Natiello |first1=Mario A. |last2=Solari |first2=Hernan Gustavo |title=On the removal of infinities from divergent series |journal=[[Philosophy of Mathematics Education Journal]] |volume=29 |date=July 2015 |pages=1–11 |hdl = 11336/46148}}.</ref>

== Physics ==
In [[bosonic string theory]], the attempt is to compute the possible energy levels of a string, in particular, the lowest energy level. Speaking informally, each harmonic of the string can be viewed as a collection of {{math|''D'' − 2}} independent [[quantum harmonic oscillator]]s, one for each [[transverse wave|transverse direction]], where {{mvar|D}} is the dimension of spacetime. If the fundamental oscillation frequency is {{mvar|ω}}, then the energy in an oscillator contributing to the {{mvar|n}}th harmonic is {{math|''nħω''/2}}. So using the divergent series, the sum over all harmonics is {{math|−''ħω''(''D'' − 2)/24}}. Ultimately it is this fact, combined with the [[Goddard–Thorn theorem]], which leads to bosonic string theory failing to be consistent in dimensions other than 26.<ref>{{Citation |first=Bernardo |last=Barbiellini |date=1987 |title=The Casimir effect in conformal field theories |journal= Physics Letters B |volume=190 |issue=1–2 |pages=137–139 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(87)90854-9 |bibcode=1987PhLB..190..137B }}.</ref>

The regularization of {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} is also involved in computing the [[Casimir force#Derivation of Casimir effect assuming zeta-regularization|Casimir force]] for a [[scalar field]] in one dimension.<ref>See [[v:Quantum mechanics/Casimir effect in one dimension]].{{unreliable source?|date=May 2021}}</ref> An exponential cutoff function suffices to smooth the series, representing the fact that arbitrarily high-energy modes are not blocked by the conducting plates. The spatial symmetry of the problem is responsible for canceling the quadratic term of the expansion. All that is left is the constant term −1/12, and the negative sign of this result reflects the fact that the Casimir force is attractive.{{sfn|Zee|2003|loc=pp. 65–67}}

A similar calculation is involved in three dimensions, using the [[Real analytic Eisenstein series#Epstein zeta function|Epstein zeta-function]] in place of the Riemann zeta function.<ref>{{citation |title=Quantum Field Theory I: Basics in Mathematics and Physics: A Bridge between Mathematicians and Physicists |first=Eberhard |last=Zeidler |publisher=Springer |year=2007 |isbn=9783540347644 |pages=305–306 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XYtnGl9enNgC&pg=PA305 |bibcode=2006qftb.book.....Z}}.</ref>

== History ==
It is unclear whether Leonhard Euler summed the series to {{sfrac|−|1|12}}. According to [[Morris Kline]], Euler's early work on divergent series relied on function expansions, from which he concluded {{math|1=1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯ = ∞}}.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Morris |last=Kline |author-link=Morris Kline |date=November 1983 |title=Euler and Infinite Series |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=56 |issue=5 |pages=307–314 |doi=10.2307/2690371|jstor=2690371 }}.</ref> According to Raymond Ayoub, the fact that the divergent zeta series is not Abel-summable prevented Euler from using the zeta function as freely as the eta function, and he "could not have attached a meaning" to the series.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Raymond |last=Ayoub |date=December 1974 |title=Euler and the Zeta Function |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=81 |issue=10 |pages=1067–1086 |url=http://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/upload_library/22/Ford/RaymondAyoub.pdf |access-date=February 14, 2014 |doi=10.2307/2319041 |jstor=2319041 }}.</ref> Other authors have credited Euler with the sum, suggesting that Euler would have extended the relationship between the zeta and eta functions to negative integers.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lefort |first=Jean |title=Les séries divergentes chez Euler |language=fr |journal=L'Ouvert |publisher=IREM de Strasbourg |issue=31 |pages=15–25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222164751/http://irem.u-strasbg.fr/php/articles/31_Lefort_divergent.pdf |archive-date=February 22, 2014 |url=http://irem.u-strasbg.fr/php/articles/31_Lefort_divergent.pdf |access-date=February 14, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Masanobu |last1=Kaneko |first2=Nobushige |last2=Kurokawa |first3=Masato |last3=Wakayama |year=2003 |title=A variation of Euler's approach to values of the Riemann zeta function |journal=Kyushu Journal of Mathematics |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=175–192 |doi=10.2206/kyushujm.57.175 |arxiv=math/0206171 |s2cid=54514141 |url=http://catalog.lib.kyushu-u.ac.jp/opac/repository/100000/handle/2324/11683/57_175.pdf |access-date=January 31, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202114604/http://catalog.lib.kyushu-u.ac.jp/opac/repository/100000/handle/2324/11683/57_175.pdf |archive-date=2014-02-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first=Jonathan |last=Sondow |date=February 1994 |title=Analytic continuation of Riemann's zeta function and values at negative integers via Euler's transformation of series |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |volume=120 |issue=4 |pages=421–424 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1994-1172954-7 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1994-120-02/S0002-9939-1994-1172954-7/ |access-date=February 14, 2014 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In the primary literature, the series {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} is mentioned in Euler's 1760 publication {{lang|la|De seriebus divergentibus}} alongside the divergent geometric series {{math|[[1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ⋯]]}}. Euler hints that series of this type have finite, negative sums, and he explains what this means for geometric series, but he does not return to discuss {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}}. In the same publication, Euler writes that the sum of {{math|[[1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯]]}} is infinite.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=E. J. |last1=Barbeau |first2=P. J. |last2=Leah |date=May 1976 |title=Euler's 1760 paper on divergent series |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=141–160 |doi=10.1016/0315-0860(76)90030-6|doi-access= }}</ref>

== In popular media ==
[[David Leavitt]]'s 2007 novel ''[[The Indian Clerk]]'' includes a scene where Hardy and [[John Edensor Littlewood|Littlewood]] discuss the meaning of this series. They conclude that Ramanujan has rediscovered {{math|''ζ''(−1)}}, and they take the "lunatic asylum" line in his second letter as a sign that Ramanujan is toying with them.<ref>{{Citation |first=David |last=Leavitt |author-link=David Leavitt |year=2007 |title=The Indian Clerk |publisher=Bloomsbury |pages=61–62}}.</ref>

[[Simon McBurney]]'s 2007 play ''[[A Disappearing Number]]'' focuses on the series in the opening scene. The main character, Ruth, walks into a lecture hall and introduces the idea of a divergent series before proclaiming, "I'm going to show you something really thrilling", namely {{math|1=1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯ = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}}. As Ruth launches into a derivation of the functional equation of the zeta function, another actor addresses the audience, admitting that they are actors: "But the mathematics is real. It's terrifying, but it's real."<ref>{{cite book |first=Simon |last=McBurney |date=April 2012 |title=A Disappearing Number |publisher=Oberon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SYkHEAAAQBAJ |isbn=9781849432993 }}.</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Rachel |last=Thomas |date=December 1, 2008 |title=A disappearing number |work=Plus |url=http://plus.maths.org/content/disappearing-number |access-date=February 5, 2014}}</ref>

In January 2014, [[Numberphile]] produced a [[YouTube]] video on the series, which gathered over 1.5&nbsp;million views in its first month.<ref name="NYT-20140203">{{cite news |first=Dennis |last=Overbye |author-link=Dennis Overbye |title=In the End, It All Adds Up to –1/12 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/04/science/in-the-end-it-all-adds-up-to.html |date=February 3, 2014 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=February 3, 2014 }}.</ref> The 8-minute video is narrated by Tony Padilla, a physicist at the [[University of Nottingham]]. Padilla begins with {{math|1 − 1 + 1 − 1 + ⋯}} and {{math|1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯}} and relates the latter to {{math|1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯}} using a term-by-term subtraction similar to Ramanujan's argument.<ref>{{YouTube |id=w-I6XTVZXww |title=ASTOUNDING: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ⋯ = –1/12}}.</ref> Numberphile also released a 21-minute version of the video featuring Nottingham physicist [[Edmund Copeland|Ed Copeland]], who describes in more detail how {{math|1=1 − 2 + 3 − 4 + ⋯ = {{sfrac|1|4}}}} as an Abel sum, and {{math|1=1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ⋯ = {{sfrac|−|1|12}}}} as {{math|''ζ''(−1)}}.<ref>{{YouTube |id=E-d9mgo8FGk |title=Sum of Natural Numbers (second proof and extra footage)}}.</ref> After receiving complaints about the lack of rigour in the first video, Padilla also wrote an explanation on his webpage relating the manipulations in the video to identities between the analytic continuations of the relevant Dirichlet series.<ref>{{cite web |first=Tony |last=Padilla |title=What do we get if we sum all the natural numbers? |url=http://www.nottingham.ac.uk/~ppzap4/response.html |access-date=February 3, 2014 |archive-date=September 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210912051044/https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/~ppzap4/response.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In ''[[The New York Times]]'' coverage of the Numberphile video, mathematician [[Edward Frenkel]] commented: "This calculation is one of the best-kept secrets in math. No one on the outside knows about it."<ref name="NYT-20140203" />

Coverage of this topic in [[Smithsonian (magazine)|''Smithsonian'' magazine]] describes the Numberphile video as misleading and notes that the interpretation of the sum as {{sfrac|−|1|12}} relies on a specialized meaning for the ''equals'' sign, from the techniques of [[analytic continuation]], in which ''equals'' means ''is associated with''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/great-debate-over-whether-1234-112-180949559/ |title=The Great Debate Over Whether 1 + 2 + 3 + 4... + ∞ = −1/12 |last=Schultz |first=Colin |date=2014-01-31 |website=Smithsonian |access-date=2016-05-16}}</ref> The Numberphile video was critiqued on similar grounds by German mathematician [[Burkard Polster]] on his ''Mathologer'' YouTube channel in 2018, his video receiving 2.7 million views by 2023.<ref>{{cite AV media |last=Polster |first=Burkard |date=January 13, 2018 |title=Numberphile v. Math: the truth about 1+2+3+⋯=−1/12 |type= |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YuIIjLr6vUA |access-date=August 31, 2023 |via=YouTube}}</ref>
